Widow Sells the 1971 Dodge Challenger Parked Outside Since 1985, Restoration "Technically Possible"
34 photos
Photo: eBay seller poundshort
Don’t do it. I know you’re tempted to click the photos in the gallery, but don’t do it. Because if you do, there’s a good chance you’ll walk away instantly, without getting a chance to discover this 1971 Dodge Challenger.
I admit that most people would consider it a wreck, a rust bucket, or a flower pot, but I’m with the seller this time. A restoration is still “technically possible,” the man states, and I don’t think this is wishful thinking. This Challenger is rough, but really now, we’ve all seen many cars in horrible shape getting a second chance, so why shouldn’t this once-Plum Crazy specimen have the same fate?
That’s right, you’ve heard it correctly. This Challenger left the factory wearing the eye-candy Plum Crazy , but the car was the subject of a series of unfortunate decisions that turned it into the pile of rusty metal that you can see in the photos here.
Photo: eBay seller poundshort It’s no secret that the 1971 Challenger was struggling with an unwelcoming market, mainly due to the insurance costs and regulations aimed at models with big muscle. The dropping sales were barely surprising, but the level of the collapse wasn’t necessarily easy to digest.
The Challenger fell from over 83,000 cars sold in the previous year to only 29,883 units.
Dodge tried to find a way to deal with the new market trends, so the Challenger was available only in three series and four models.
The two-door hardtop was the configuration that dominated the series, accounting for over 23,000 orders. This made sense, considering it was also the most affordable, carrying a base price of $2,858 for the version fitted with a six-cylinder engine - yes, a six was still offered, but most Challenger buyers agreed that this didn’t make much sense; fewer than 2,000 cars got a six.
The R/T accounted for 4,630 orders, while the convertible was the rarest with 2,165 buyers.
Photo: eBay seller poundshort Dodge offered a wide variety of engines, but the Challenger was already prepared for big changes for the following model year. This was the last year for the Hemi, so 191 was the last opportunity to pay $790 for the massive 425-horsepower upgrade.
The Challenger lineup included 18 colors, with five high-impact configurations . Hemi Orange and Plum Crazy were and still are the most desirable.
Unfortunately, this Challenger no longer wears the original Plum Crazy treatment.
“The second owner bought this car and painted it blue,” the seller reveals. That’s a sad change, not just because Plum Crazy was such a fantastic color, but also because it pushed the car further away from its original setup. The blue finish certainly doesn’t look as good as Plum Crazy, though it’s fair to admit that its current condition doesn’t help either.
I don’t think it makes sense to dissect its condition because it’s pretty clear that this Challenger requires extensive work in every single regard. There’s a lot of rust, but the owner says there are also solid sections.
“It has some rare and nice parts, including the whole convertible top mechanism, which is very solid, and intact rear window glass,” they reveal.
Photo: eBay seller poundshort An engine is no longer in the car, but this isn’t necessarily bad news. It’s been sitting for so long and in horrible conditions that an engine would have only been seized.
“I was told that it was originally a 318 engine car,” the seller says. So you’re not missing anything special, though the factory 318 unit would have helped the bravest souls out there keep the car original.
As for the car’s overall condition, we should just blame the rainy days for it.
“It sat outside since 1985, and while it was covered by tarps, they long since decayed, and the car was exposed to weather and moisture. The owner passed away, and I purchased it from his widow,” the seller explains.
That’s why the rust damage is massive. The floor pan is no more, and the seller notes that “the frame and the underbody are not visible.”
Photo: eBay seller poundshort This is a major project, by all means, and my recommendation is that you go there in person to see it with your eyes if you somehow believe it’s worth your time and money. The owner lives in Epping, New Hampshire, and you’ll obviously need a trailer to take it home because there’s no chance you’ll get this car on its wheels otherwise. The front wheels are frozen, but the rear ones still turn.
As for the price, it’s pretty clear that you can’t pay high dollars for this Challenger. That’s why the owner decided to let a no-reserve auction decide the price, though the starting bid could end up keeping people away.
To join the digital fight, you must pay at least $4,976, and so far, nobody has done so, despite over 20 users adding the Challenger to their watchlists. The auction ends in 5 days.
